📚 Today you learned

IV Crush

Implied volatility (IV) is priced up going into a known binary event — NVDA into tomorrow's print is a clean live example, with options pricing in roughly a 7-9% move historically. The moment the news hits and uncertainty resolves, IV collapses back to normal levels regardless of which way the stock moves. That collapse — the "crush" — destroys extrinsic option value on its own, separate from price direction. A trader who buys a call the day before NVDA earnings expecting a pop can be right on direction and still lose money, because the stock has to move MORE than the IV-implied move just to offset the crush. This is why buying options into binary catalysts is a much harder trade than it looks — you're not just betting on direction, you're betting the actual move beats what's already priced in. It's the same logic that burned the CAPR/VERA/CELC binary-catalyst trades on the equity side, just expressed through options pricing instead of a stock gap.

Also today: Extrinsic value — the part of an option's price that isn't intrinsic (strike vs. spot); this is exactly what IV crush destroys.
